description: We are Erebus Computatrum, a dynamic duo tackling the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge for the Universal 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. We specialize in software development and data visualization, fueled by a deep passion for lunar exploration. While our team is set, we are eager to connect, exchange ideas, and build a stellar, high-impact space app together for this amazing hackathon event. Let's make an impact!
summary:
SouthLight is a web app that answers one question for any lunar landing site and date: will a lander get sunlight for power, and can it see Earth for direct radio contact?

At the Moon's south pole the Sun only skims the horizon and Earth wobbles behind mountains, so moving a lander a few kilometres or landing a few days late can decide whether it survives. NASA's expert tools contain this information, but they are slow to use for quick "what if" questions.

SouthLight rebuilds each site in 3D from NASA LRO LOLA terrain, lit by the real Sun and Earth positions from NASA/JPL SPICE ephemeris, and gives a plain-language verdict. A 30-day timeline shows power and radio windows with countdowns to sunset and Earthset; a launch-delay slider and a Plan B finder search nearby sites and dates; a seasons view shows the best months; and Launch mode lets anyone fly a virtual lander on the real data and get a safety score with reasons. Our Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons to within 0.0001°. It helps mission planners decide fast and helps students and the public understand why the Moon's south pole is so hard.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SouthLight turns NASA ephemeris and topography data into fast, visual answers for lunar landing-site planning. It has three modes.

Explore (students and the public):

- Pick a curated site (Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton/IM-2, de Gerlache rim, Shackleton crater floor, IM-1, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e 4, Apollo 11 and 17) or tap anywhere on a south-pole map coloured by yearly sunlight, Earth visibility, slope or elevation.

- A realistic 3D view rebuilds the site from NASA LOLA terrain at true scale, lit by the Sun from its real direction, so the shadows are the real shadows for that date and hour. Earth is lit by the same Sun, so its phase is correct. Astronaut view lets you stand on the ground and look around; Drone view lets you fly over the craters.

- "Move site 2 km" shows how much a short move changes sunlight. A guided tour and a plain-English verdict explain everything.

Plan (mission planners):

- 30-day hour-by-hour timeline of sunlight (power) and Earth visibility (direct radio), with countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset.

- Launch-delay slider, month-by-month seasons chart, site comparison table, and CSV export.

- Plan B finder: tests every terrain-grid point within 10 km and landing times up to 10 days later, then ranks them for the chosen lander.

Launch (everyone):

- Choose a small, medium or large lander and launch it. The mission is simulated hour by hour on the real data: solar power and battery, Earth contact, landing in light or darkness, slope, and a rocket-equation fuel budget. The result is a Mission Safety Score with plain-language reasons. Any scenario can be shared as a link.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Python + SpiceyPy with NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440) compute the apparent Sun and Earth positions seen from the Moon every hour (Nov 2026 to Dec 2028). The browser converts them into azimuth and elevation for any site.

2. Following the published method of Mazarico et al. (2011), we march outward in every direction across NASA LRO LOLA elevation models (40 m and 240 m polar maps, and the global LDEM_64) to find each site's true horizon, including the Moon's curvature. The Moon has no air, so the horizon is purely terrain.

3. We precomputed horizons, slopes and 2027 statistics for about 17,700 south-pole points on a 2 km grid, plus 3D terrain tiles; the website loads only what it needs.

4. The website is HTML/CSS/JavaScript with three.js for 3D, hosted free on GitHub Pages. All code is open source on GitHub.

VALIDATION

- Sun and Earth positions match the JPL Horizons API to within 0.0001°.

- Sunlight agrees with published studies: the Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge gets 81–93% sunlight in 2027; Shackleton's floor gets 0% (a permanently shadowed region).

IMPACT

When hardware problems or launch delays force a change, a team can see in seconds how a new date or site affects power and communication, and find a Plan B. The same tool shows students and the public why the lunar south pole is so challenging.

CREATIVITY

Most tools show tables. SouthLight lets you stand on the real terrain, watch the Sun disappear behind a mountain, then try to keep a lander alive.

LIMITS

Educational and planning-support tool, not for mission certification. Terrain resolution is 40–470 m; lander models are simplified and generic.

USE OF AI

The team chose the challenge, concept, audience and features. Code was written with the help of an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) and checked against JPL Horizons and published studies. No AI-generated images, audio or video.
